bullets: How friction fights a slide yet can drive a car, how a force times its distance from a pivot makes a moment, and how the same force spread over a smaller area makes a bigger pressure
slides.heading: Forces: friction, moments and pressure
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we push one block, balance one beam and stand one crate on its edge, and learn to read forces by what they do.

bullets: Find the net force when friction opposes a push, and say why friction opposes relative slide rather than motion itself
Calculate a moment as force times distance from the pivot, and a pressure as force over area
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: You stand flat, then rise on tiptoes - your weight pushing on the floor has not changed at all
So is the pressure under your feet the same, or has it grown?
slides.heading: Same push - same pressure?
slides.notes: Ask for predictions and take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: the pressure scene will settle it.

bullets: Friction opposes the relative slide between two surfaces; a moment is a force times its distance from the pivot; pressure is a force spread over an area
Each quantity is a ratio or a product: change one part and the whole effect changes, even when the force itself stays the same
slides.heading: Friction, moments and pressure
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the map for the whole lesson: first the slide, then the turn, then the spread.

bullets: A 60-newton push drives the block right while a 40-newton friction arrow grows at the contact, pointing back against the slide
The net force is 20 newtons to the right, so the block keeps sliding - friction fights the slide, not the push
slides.heading: Friction opposes relative motion
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: follow the block, watch the friction arrow appear at the contact, and name the net force that survives.

bullets: On the left, 60 newtons at 0.5 metres from the pivot makes a moment of 30 newton-metres; on the right, 30 newtons at 0.75 metres makes only 22.5, so the beam tips left
The right weight slides out to 1.0 metre: 30 times 1.0 is 30 newton-metres, the moments match, and the beam levels
slides.heading: Moments: force times distance from the pivot
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: read each moment off as force times distance, watch the beam tip, then watch the slide outward restore the balance.

bullets: A 200-newton crate rests on its wide face: area 0.5 square metres, so the pressure is 400 pascals and the dent stays shallow
The same crate tips onto its narrow edge: area 0.05 square metres, one tenth as much, so the pressure is 4000 pascals and the dent deepens
slides.heading: Pressure: the same force on different areas
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: the force never changes, only the area shrinks - and the pressure reading climbs tenfold.

bullets: A driving wheel rolls forward while its contact patch pushes backward on the road
The road pushes back: friction on the tyre points forward, so here friction drives the car - it opposes the relative slide, not the motion
slides.heading: Check the thinking
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: follow the tyre push backward, then the friction arrow forward, and name the slide friction is really opposing.

bullets: A 200 N crate on its wide face: pressure = force / area = 200 / 0.5 = 400 Pa
The same crate on its narrow edge: pressure = 200 / 0.05 = 4000 Pa - ten times the area down, ten times the pressure up
slides.heading: Worked example: one crate, two pressures
slides.notes: Work this on the board slowly: write the formula, divide for the wide face, then change only the area and divide again.

bullets: A beam has 40 newtons at 0.25 metres on one side - find its moment, then say where a 20-newton weight must sit on the other side to balance it
Then open the worksheet: one net-force reading, one tiptoe trap and two calculations
slides.heading: Your turn
slides.notes: Give three quiet minutes for the first task, take answers from the class, then set the worksheet going in pairs.

bullets: Four questions: the tiptoe pressure trap, a moment balance, a pressure calculation, and friction that drives a car
Write one sentence: why does standing on tiptoes raise the pressure under your feet when your weight is unchanged?
slides.heading: Exit ticket
slides.notes: Collect the tickets at the door; the first question revisits the trap head-on, so it shows straight away who still thinks the same push must mean the same pressure.
